structure.title: A family displaced
structure.text: Loss of home changes the sisters' circumstances and makes their different emotional habits visible.

structure.title: Judging attentions
structure.text: Courtships, visits, and withheld information test what appearances can establish about another person's intentions.

people.name: Elinor Dashwood
people.text: The eldest Dashwood daughter, who keeps her feelings to herself and looks after her family's affairs when their fortunes suddenly shrink.

people.name: Marianne Dashwood
people.text: Elinor's younger sister, who believes love should be all-consuming and says exactly what she feels, whoever is listening.

people.name: Their mother
people.text: Mrs Dashwood, newly widowed and moved out of her home, warm and impulsive, more like Marianne than like Elinor.

context.title: Inheritance and security
context.text: The family's changed income makes hospitality, marriage, and housing interdependent. Financial calculation is part of the emotional story.
context.takeaway: Affection does not remove material dependence.

context.title: Two habits, not two boxes
context.text: The sisters both think and feel. The contrast concerns expression and judgment rather than a division into a rational person and an emotional one.

notice.text: Follow private feelings withheld from family.
notice.why: Silence can protect others while deepening isolation.
Polite reasoning can make selfishness appear inevitable.

opening: The Dashwood sisters lose their home, and their well-off relatives find excellent reasons not to help very much. Elinor tries to keep the family steady; Marianne regards restraint as a poor substitute for feeling deeply. Both encounter men whose attentions are easier to interpret hopefully than accurately. Austen makes the courtship funny without forgetting its financial consequences, following what can happen when a woman must discover someone's intentions through visits, silences, and rumours while having very little power to demand a straightforward answer.
